pharm: Macrolide calcineurin inhibitor; binds FKBP-12 to inhibit calcineurin phosphatase and T-cell activation
tags: Boxed warning: malignancies and serious infections

Take consistently with or without food; avoid grapefruit

Present in human milk; weigh benefits against infant risk
PK unchanged but nephrotoxic; use lower end of range with pre-existing impairment
Severe impairment (Child-Pugh >=10) reduces clearance; lower doses, monitor closely
Whole blood trough (TDM), renal function, K+, glucose, BP, Mg
summary: Tacrolimus is a calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant indicated for prophylaxis of organ rejection in kidney, liver, heart, and lung transplant recipients, given orally or by continuous IV infusion in combination with other immunosuppressants. It has a narrow therapeutic index requiring whole-blood trough therapeutic drug monitoring, and causes nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hyperkalemia, hypertension, and new-onset diabetes. It carries a boxed warning for increased risk of serious infections and malignancies (including lymphoma and skin cancer). A separate topical ointment is approved as second-line therapy for atopic dermatitis and carries its own boxed warning about a theoretical malignancy risk.

admin: Should be prescribed only under supervision of a physician experienced in immunosuppressive therapy and transplant management
Take oral doses at the same 12-hour intervals daily, consistently with or without food (food lowers bioavailability)
Do not eat grapefruit or drink grapefruit juice with tacrolimus
Do not use simultaneously with cyclosporine; separate by at least 24 hours
Immediate-release (Prograf) is NOT interchangeable/substitutable with extended-release tacrolimus products; changes require physician supervision
IV use only as continuous infusion; observe patient for at least the first 30 minutes for anaphylaxis with epinephrine available at bedside
Granules for oral suspension: mix in glass cup with 15-30 mL room-temperature water, give immediately, use non-PVC equipment; do not sprinkle on food
Capsules should not be opened or crushed; wear gloves when handling granules/injection (fetal harm risk)
moa: Tacrolimus binds the intracellular protein FKBP-12, forming a complex with calcium, calmodulin, and calcineurin that inhibits calcineurin's phosphatase activity. This prevents dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of transcription factors (e.g., NF-AT, NF-kB), suppressing production of cytokines including IL-2 and interferon-gamma. The net effect is inhibition of T-lymphocyte activation and proliferation, producing immunosuppression.

absolute: PROGRAF injection: hypersensitivity to HCO-60 (polyoxyl 60 hydrogenated castor oil)

Topical ointment: immunocompromised patients, use under occlusion, first-line use

EBV serology / signs of infection or malignancy

preg: Tacrolimus can cause fetal harm. Postmarketing and registry (TPRI) data show increased risk of prematurity (<37 weeks), birth defects/congenital anomalies, low birth weight (<2500 g), and fetal distress; renal dysfunction and transient neonatal hyperkalemia have been reported at delivery. May worsen maternal hyperglycemia and hypertension/pre-eclampsia. Background major-birth-defect risk in the US general population is 2-4%. Advise of risk; encourage enrollment in the Transplantation Pregnancy Registry International (1-877-955-6877).
lact: Tacrolimus is present in human milk; controlled human lactation studies have not been conducted and effects on the breastfed infant or milk production are unknown. In animal studies postnatal exposure caused developmental toxicity. Weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding and the mother's clinical need against potential infant risk.
renal: Tacrolimus pharmacokinetics are similar in renal impairment to normal renal function, but the drug is nephrotoxic. In liver, heart, or lung transplant patients with pre-existing renal impairment, dose at the lower end of the therapeutic range; further reductions below target may be needed. In kidney transplant patients with post-operative oliguria, give the first dose no sooner than 6 h and within 24 h of transplant, or delay until renal recovery. Not significantly dialyzable.
hepatic: Patients with severe hepatic impairment (mean Child-Pugh >=10) have substantially reduced clearance and prolonged half-life and may require lower doses with close trough monitoring. Liver transplant recipients with post-transplant hepatic impairment are at increased risk of renal insufficiency from high whole-blood concentrations; monitor closely and consider dose reduction.

major: Strong CYP3A inhibitors - protease inhibitors (telaprevir, boceprevir, ritonavir, nelfinavir), azole antifungals (voriconazole, posaconazole, itraconazole, ketoconazole), clarithromycin, nefazodone, letermovir (markedly raise tacrolimus levels - reduce dose, e.g. one-third dose with voriconazole/posaconazole, monitor closely)
Strong CYP3A inducers - rifampin, rifabutin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort (lower levels, rejection risk - increase dose, monitor)
Nephrotoxic drugs - aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, ganciclovir, cisplatin, NRTIs, protease inhibitors (additive nephrotoxicity)
QT-prolonging drugs / amiodarone (additive QT prolongation, Torsades de pointes risk)
Sirolimus in liver/heart transplant (excess mortality, graft loss, hepatic artery thrombosis, TMA - not recommended)
Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs (additive hyperkalemia)
moderate: Mild/moderate CYP3A inhibitors - erythromycin, fluconazole, clotrimazole, calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, nicardipine), danazol, cimetidine, lansoprazole, omeprazole, ethinyl estradiol (raise levels)
Magnesium/aluminum hydroxide antacids and metoclopramide (raise levels)
Mild/moderate CYP3A inducers - methylprednisolone, prednisone, caspofungin (lower levels)
Mycophenolic acid products (tacrolimus increases MPA exposure vs cyclosporine - monitor MPA toxicity)
minor: Direct-acting antiviral HCV therapy (altered PK via changing liver function - monitor)
interactions.food: Food (especially high-fat meals) decreases rate and extent of absorption; take consistently with or without food. Grapefruit/grapefruit juice is a CYP3A inhibitor that raises trough levels - avoid.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid grapefruit/grapefruit juice; limit alcohol given hepatic involvement and additive toxicity potential.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum creatinine, potassium, glucose/HbA1c, and lipids; may decrease magnesium. Immunoassay trough results can read higher than HPLC/MS due to metabolite cross-reactivity.

serious: Neurotoxicity including PRES, seizure, delirium, coma
Serious/opportunistic infections (BK virus nephropathy, CMV, PML)
Lymphoma and other malignancies (incl. skin, PTLD)
emergency: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) / seizure / coma

monitoring: Whole blood trough tacrolimus concentrations (TDM) - most frequent during first week post-transplant and after interacting-drug changes
Renal function (serum creatinine) and urine output
Blood glucose / HbA1c (new-onset diabetes; higher risk in African-American and Hispanic patients)
ECG and electrolytes (Mg, K, Ca) in patients with QT risk factors
Signs of infection and EBV serology (PTLD risk)
Skin examination for malignancy; CBC for cytopenias; echocardiography if ventricular dysfunction or renal failure develops
counsel: Take at the same 12-hour intervals daily, consistently with or without food
Confirm your medicine looks the same at each refill - other tacrolimus (extended-release) products are not substitutable
You are at increased risk of infections and of cancers (especially skin) - report fever, chills, cough, or skin changes; limit sun/UV exposure, wear protective clothing and use high-SPF sunscreen
Report increased thirst/urination/hunger (diabetes), vision changes, delirium, tremor, or unusual bruising/bleeding
Tell all providers before starting or stopping any prescription, OTC, herbal, or supplement product, and avoid live vaccines
Discuss contraception and family planning; tacrolimus can harm a fetus and may affect fertility
Attend all visits and blood tests for drug-level and organ monitoring
pk: Immunosuppressive effect develops over days; absorption incomplete and variable (oral bioavailability ~17-22%)
~31-35 hours in healthy volunteers; ~11-19 hours in transplant patients; prolonged in severe hepatic impairment
Twice-daily dosing (every 12 hours); extensive CYP3A4/3A5 metabolism, <1% excreted unchanged (mainly fecal)
Capsules and granules: 20-25 C (68-77 F), excursions 15-30 C. Injection: store 5-25 C (41-77 F); diluted infusion discard after 24 h, use non-PVC containers
pearls: Narrow therapeutic index - whole-blood trough TDM is essential to balance rejection against toxicity (nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity)
A strong CYP3A inhibitor (e.g., clarithromycin) can cause a rapid, sharp rise in levels despite preemptive dose reduction - start trough monitoring within 1-3 days
Immediate-release tacrolimus is NOT interchangeable with extended-release products - dispensing errors have caused graft rejection or toxicity
Avoid combining with sirolimus in liver and heart transplant; avoid in congenital long QT syndrome; do not co-administer with cyclosporine
African-American patients often need higher doses for comparable troughs and are at higher risk of new-onset diabetes after transplant

Topical tacrolimus (Protopic) details derive from the separate FDA Protopic ointment label, not this Prograf systemic source; it is second-line for atopic dermatitis and carries its own boxed warning on theoretical malignancy risk
missed: Take the missed oral dose as soon as remembered to keep consistent 12-hour spacing; if it is close to the next scheduled dose, skip it and resume the regular schedule. Do not double the dose. Granules for suspension must be given immediately after preparation. Contact the transplant team about repeated missed doses, as under-exposure risks rejection.
overdose: Experience is limited; acute overdoses up to 30 times the intended dose have been reported, mostly asymptomatic with full recovery. Reactions may mirror known adverse effects - tremor, abnormal renal function, hypertension, peripheral edema, and (in one case) transient urticaria and lethargy. Tacrolimus is not significantly dialyzable due to high erythrocyte/protein binding; activated charcoal has been used but is not routinely recommended. Management is general supportive care and treatment of specific symptoms.
